Let’s step into Chapter 6: Redesigning Products for the Segment of One.
Picture this: you’re sitting in a product design meeting. The old way of thinking—just build one thing for everyone—still hangs in the air. But then, someone asks, “What if we could make this fit each person, not just the average?” Suddenly, the room feels different. There’s a spark, a sense of possibility, and maybe a little bit of fear, too.
Take the story of a team at a consumer electronics company. They were proud of their best-selling headphones. But as customer reviews came in, a pattern started to show. Some folks loved the fit, but others? Not so much. Instead of brushing off the complaints, the team leaned in and listened. They realized, comfort isn’t one-size-fits-all.
So, what did they do? They started offering adjustable headbands, swappable ear pads, and even an online quiz to help people find their perfect match. Suddenly, returns dropped, reviews turned positive, and customers felt like these headphones had been made just for them.
That’s a big shift—from designing for the crowd, to designing for the individual. It takes a new kind of thinking. You’ve got to see the real person behind the purchase. Imagine their daily routine. Ask yourself—what would make life easier, more delightful, or just plain better for them?
Here’s the thing—most companies don’t realize just how much room there is to adapt. Sometimes it’s as simple as letting people pick a color, or add a personal engraving. Other times, it might mean rethinking the whole product experience.
Here’s another example. A meal delivery service had a menu that worked for most people. But then, more and more customers started asking for gluten-free, vegan, or low-sodium choices. At first, the company hesitated—customization sounded expensive and complicated. But as those requests kept coming, they realized ignoring them meant losing business.
So, they changed. They built a flexible menu system, letting customers create meals that fit their needs. The kitchen had to adapt, sure. But it paid off. People felt heard—and they told their friends.
Redesigning for the segment of one isn’t about giving endless options or making things complicated. It’s about thoughtful choices—really listening, learning, and making small tweaks that add up to something huge.
The companies that thrive? They’re the ones who treat every complaint and every suggestion as a peek into what people truly want.
It’s tempting to just stick with what’s always worked. But the world’s changing. People want more, and honestly, they’re willing to pay for it. The future? It belongs to those bold enough to ask, “How can we make this truly yours?”
